a: Memory the CPU can access directly, holding data and instructions in use
Long-term storage for files you aren't using
tasks.fb: RAM, ROM, cache and registers are all primary storage.

tasks.q: Why are programs copied into RAM before they run?
a: RAM is much faster than secondary storage, so the CPU doesn't have to wait
RAM is bigger than a hard drive
RAM keeps data when the power is off
tasks.fb: Speed is the whole reason primary storage exists.

a: The contents are lost when the power is switched off
It can explode if it gets hot
tasks.fb: That's why unsaved work disappears in a power cut.

tasks.q: Which is stored in RAM while a computer is running?
a: The operating system and the programs currently open
Files you haven't opened for years
tasks.fb: Anything being used is copied into RAM.

a: The start-up instructions, often called the BIOS
tasks.fb: ROM holds the small program that gets everything else started.

tasks.q: Why is ROM used for the boot program?
a: It is non-volatile, so the instructions are still there when the power comes on
It can be written to easily
tasks.fb: If it were in RAM it would be empty at switch-on.

tasks.q: Does each statement describe RAM or ROM?
items: Volatile: loses its contents at power off
Can be read from and written to
Can normally only be read from
Holds the operating system while the computer runs
Holds the BIOS or boot program
tasks.fb: Both are primary storage, but they do very different jobs.

tasks.q: Put the start-up steps in order.
steps: The CPU runs the boot program stored in ROM
The BIOS checks the hardware is working
The operating system is copied from secondary storage into RAM
tasks.fb: This is why both types of primary storage are needed.

tasks.q: Why does a computer slow down when RAM is full?
a: It has to use much slower secondary storage as extra memory
tasks.fb: That's virtual memory, which is the next lesson.

tasks.q: A computer has plenty of free RAM but still feels slow. What does adding more RAM do?
a: Very little: the bottleneck is somewhere else
tasks.fb: More RAM only helps when RAM is the limit.

info.title: Core memory
info.text: Early computers used 'core memory': tiny magnetic rings threaded on wires by hand. A few kilobytes filled a cabinet.

info.title: How fast?
info.text: RAM can be read in tens of nanoseconds. A hard disk takes milliseconds, which is around a hundred thousand times longer.

info.title: Flashable ROM
info.text: Modern boot ROM is usually flash memory, so it can be updated. That's what a 'BIOS update' or 'firmware update' does.

info.title: Why 'random access'?
info.text: Any location in RAM can be reached just as quickly as any other. Tape, by contrast, has to be wound to the right place.

info.title: RAM in phones
info.text: Phones have RAM too, usually 4 GB to 12 GB. It's why a phone with more RAM can keep more apps open in the background.

info.title: Power cuts
info.text: Some servers keep a battery-backed cache, so data in memory isn't lost if the power fails before it's written to disk.
